find: Federal drug agents enter a New York apartment without a warrant, manacle the tenant in front of his family, threaten them, search the apartment, and strip-search the tenant at a federal facility. The tenant sues the agents for damages under the Fourth Amendment. The facts track \textit{Bivens} itself, which \textit{Egbert} declined to overrule, so a court could hold the claim arises in no new context. But \textit{Egbert} warned that ``parallel circumstances'' with \textit{Bivens} are not enough unless the claim also survives the Court's restrictive modern framework, and the agency's internal complaint process might count as an alternative remedial structure. Justice Gorsuch saw no principled way to distinguish such cases. Whether even a \textit{Bivens} replica survives is uncertain.
replace: Federal narcotics agents assigned to a joint federal--state task force arrest a tenant in his New York apartment without a warrant or probable cause, manacle him in front of his family, search the apartment, and strip-search him at a federal facility. The tenant sues the federal agents for damages under the Fourth Amendment. The alleged search and arrest closely track \textit{Bivens}, and the plaintiff can argue that the agents acted in their ordinary federal narcotics-enforcement role. If the task force gave the agents a materially different legal mandate or supplied a distinct remedial process, a court could find a new context and decline to extend \textit{Bivens}. Whether the task-force assignment made a meaningful difference would turn on the facts.
reason: Egbert's reference to parallel circumstances addresses extension to a new context. The original example stated no meaningful factual difference from Bivens and treated modern limits on extensions as though they displaced the original holding.
source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/388/ at 389; https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/582/15-1358/ at slip op. 16; https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/596/21-147/ at slip op. 6–12, 16
